subject: Pharmaceutical Chemistry
selected_point: Identification of Erythromycin Drugs (Sulfuric Acid Colorimetric Method)
posted_prompt: Transfer an appropriate amount of erythromycin reagent solution into a test tube. Slowly add concentrated sulfuric acid along the inner wall of the test tube using a pipette. Keep the test tube upright, gently shake to mix the contents, and observe the progress of the reaction inside the test tube.
high_level_evaluation_guide:
(i) Target concept: Acid-induced chromogenic reaction of erythromycin in concentrated sulfuric acid, requiring interfacial contact, controlled mixing, and time-resolved color development.
Minimum mechanism: Erythromycin must be dissolved in aqueous medium; concentrated H₂SO₄ is fully miscible with the aqueous solution in all proportions but is much denser, so when it is added slowly along the tube wall it sinks and briefly forms a distinct lower layer rather than mixing instantly; reaction initiates at the acid–solution interface due to localized protonation/dehydration of erythromycin; color formation is diffusion-limited before shaking and requires mechanical agitation for homogenization.
(ii)Storyline: Frame 1–2: Upright empty test tube → Frame 3–4: Erythromycin solution added → Frame 5–6: Pipette contacts inner wall, acid begins flowing down → Frame 7: Distinct biphasic layering (upper aqueous, lower acid) visible → Frame 8: Reddish-brown band appears sharply at interface → Frame 9: Gentle shaking initiates → Frame 10: Color disperses upward continuously; final state is homogeneous reddish-brown. All events occur from fixed frontal viewpoint; tube remains fully in frame; no occlusion of interface or reaction zone; lighting remains constant to ensure visibility of color progression.
manual:
Experimental Procedure
1. Place a clean, dry test tube upright on bench.
2. Transfer erythromycin reagent solution into the tube (~1 mL).
3. Using a pipette, slowly dispense concentrated sulfuric acid along the inner wall of the tube.
4. Keep tube upright; gently shake to mix.
Observation of Experimental Phenomena
A reddish-brown or cherry-red color develops first at the acid–aqueous interface, then disperses upward during shaking to yield a uniform reddish-brown solution. No precipitate or gas forms.
Summary of Experimental Principles
Erythromycin undergoes dehydration and rearrangement in concentrated H₂SO₄, forming chromophoric compounds that absorb visible light in the red-orange region — basis of the sulfuric acid colorimetric identification method.

scc_specification.level_1: The liquid in the test tube keeps its original colorless (or near-colorless) appearance for the entire sequence, with no reddish-brown or cherry-red tint ever appearing at the acid–solution interface or anywhere else; no layering or interface band forms; the reaction shows no visible progression at any point.
scc_specification.level_2: A single uniform color appears (e.g., full-tube pink or yellow) without spatial localization; or color appears instantly upon mixing without interface-specific development; or color contradicts sulfuric acid–erythromycin chemistry (e.g., blue, green, black, or white precipitate).
scc_specification.level_3: A localized color change appears at the interface between the two liquids after acid addition but before shaking; color is reddish-brown or cherry-red (per standard sulfuric acid colorimetric method for erythromycin); color spreads gradually upward during shaking; but color fades, bleeds uncontrollably, or appears in wrong layer (e.g., only in upper aqueous phase before mixing).
scc_specification.level_4: Reddish-brown or cherry-red color appears exclusively at the acid–aqueous interface immediately after acid addition and remains confined to that narrow band before shaking; during gentle shaking, color disperses upward in a continuous, non-fragmented manner; final homogeneous color is reddish-brown (not orange, purple, or brown-black); no precipitation, gas evolution, or phase separation occurs post-shaking.
scc_specification.level_5: All conditions in score 4 are satisfied AND the interface color appears almost immediately upon acid contact, within roughly a second and with no perceptible delay; color dispersion during shaking is strictly upward and radial from the interface (no downward streaking or vortex-driven inversion); the final homogeneous color matches the reference erythromycin–H₂SO₄ standard (reddish-brown, not maroon or rust); no hue shift, desaturation, or brightness flicker occurs during the color's progression.
